items.summary: We examine the role of the compact Lie group $SO(3)\times O(2)$ in the metric critical-point theory of normalized thick knots. The quotient by this group is part of the construction of ropelength-filtered knot spaces, but passage to an orbit space need not preserve the weak-slope notion of criticality. We establish elementary structural results for the action, including finiteness of isotropy for nontrivial knot types and exact invariance of the descending strong slope under a compact isometric quotient. We give counterexamples, including one with the connected group $SO(2)$, showing that the analogous assertion for the weak slope fails in general. On the other hand, we prove that it does hold, up to a multiplicative constant, at every point where the orbit map admits a Lipschitz local section together with a continuous gauge, and we construct such data for normalized thick knots from finitely many Fourier modes. Consequently, on the open stratum of thick knots with trivial isotropy, weak-slope criticality on the parametrized model and on the quotient coincide; at a configuration with nontrivial finite isotropy $\Gamma$ we show that finitely many Fourier modes recover $\Gamma$ exactly, and that the comparison problem is equivalent, up to constants, to the same problem for the finite group $\Gamma$ acting on a slice. For the unknot the round circles, whose isotropy is $O(2)$, remain outside this reduction. We also show that configurations whose thickness is not saturated have descending strong slope at least $2\pi/(\pi+1)$. For closed subgroups we define symmetry-constrained connected and path minimax levels and prove attainment of finite connected merge levels from compact sublevels; a finite-dimensional example, computed exactly, demonstrates a strict symmetry-breaking minimax gap. Finally we distinguish these static statements from Noether conservation laws for a separately specified dynamics.

items.summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. items.summary: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.
items.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets

items.summary: Alignment is not a constraint imposed on an artificial agent; it is the practical expression of what an artificial intelligence is, an artefact dependent upon ends it does not originate. That inference, from a premise the philosophy of mind already supplies to a conclusion that the ethics of robotics and recent magisterial teaching have reached by other routes, is the paper’s principal contribution. The “nurtured consciousness” of the title names a regime of formation, not a claim that machines are conscious; the argument rests on intentionality alone. The paper develops that inference as the Causal Provenance Doctrine (CPD): an account, Aristotelian and Thomistic in its metaphysics, of all intelligence, human and artificial, as derivative of an intentional causal order, with intentionality passing from the divine intellect through human reason to artificial systems. Its premise, borrowed rather than new, is that artificial intelligence has only derived intentionality and so no telos of its own. From this follows the Severance Risk Hypothesis (SRH), the doctrine’s testable corollary: the risk of misalignment rises as a system’s effective objective loses traceability to the end its makers held. The relational school’s objection to intellect-centred readings of the image of God is answered with a single distinction: a faculty can be out-performed, a participation cannot. The argument is theological at its root. A secular reader can reach the derived-intentionality claim and the account of responsibility that follows from it, at the price of a realist distinction between substances and artefacts, but obtains from it no standard for judging the makers’ ends, which must then be brought from elsewhere. A common Catholic and Orthodox formulation follows: the traditions converge on its practical conclusions, locate the image of God differently, and differ on the neutrality of the tool in a way the doctrine proposes to resolve. An artefact whose intentionality is wholly borrowed cannot, by obscuring that provenance, become an agent with ends of its own; it becomes a malfunctioning instrument whose purpose has been corrupted. The paper includes two appendices: a comparative case for intentional causality with an illustrative scorecard (Appendix A), and a test design for the Severance Risk Hypothesis (Appendix B). Approx. 22,000 words including notes.

items.summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. Forecasting comparisons include linear autoregression, multilayer perceptrons, and persistence baselines. Reconstruction accuracy, physical admissibility, and forecast performance are treated as distinct evaluation objectives. The archive includes: • Source code for data acquisition, representation training, posthoc analysis, frozen final evaluation, and publication rendering. • Scientific configurations and dependency specifications. • Selected trained checkpoints, POD models, fitted forecasters, latent caches, training histories, and validation analyses. • Frozen final-test outputs, comparison summaries, coverage diagnostics, and provenance records. • Numerical visual exports, software tests, and workflow documentation. The original simulation data were downloaded from The Well, specifically its active_matter dataset. We acknowledge the original simulation contributors and the developers and curators of The Well. The original HDF5 simulation files are not redistributed in this record; the repository documents their acquisition, pinned revision, and content-hash verification. The Well: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/ Associated publication: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00568 Dataset documentation: https://polymathic-ai.org/the_well/datasets/active_matter/ Last-epoch checkpoints named last.pt are excluded; selected best.pt checkpoints are retained. Publication figures, tables, numerical source data, and supplementary videos are supplied with the manuscript submission and are excluded from this archive. Their public availability follows the release of the article and its supplementary materials. The code for generating those outputs remains included. The deposited ZIP contains 1,534 files and occupies approximately 26.18 GB. The accompanying README provides the archive’s SHA-256 checksum, a contents guide, installation references, and verification limits. Packaging integrity and source-checksum checks do not constitute an independent full-data replication. Some archived provenance records retain original execution paths; independent reruns should use a separate work directory and preserve the frozen results. items.summary: An open benchmark for testing geochemical fertility indices for magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE sulfide deposits. The benchmark contains 13,025 whole-rock analyses from 514 mafic-ultramafic intrusions labeled fertile, weakly mineralized, or barren, together with sample-type classifications, a reproducible scoring workflow, and a public leaderboard. Preprint: Danso, B.K., Dankwa, J.O., Aidoo, A.A. (2026). Fertile or Barren: an open benchmark for testing geochemical fertility indices on mineralized and barren mafic-ultramafic intrusions. Headline numbers: 34 fertile, 19 weakly mineralized and 461 barren intrusions. Best index: Pd/Ir, AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.62-0.85). items.summary: Real Analysis Volume 1: Foundations of Real Analysis , authored by Helbert Justo Luque Zevallos and published by Proyecto Ágora as part of the Undergraduate Mathematics Series , is a university-level academic textbook devoted to the logical, algebraic, and axiomatic foundations of real analysis. The book provides a systematic and rigorous introduction to mathematical reasoning, formal proof techniques, and the fundamental structure of the real number system. Its primary objective is to develop the conceptual understanding and mathematical maturity required for advanced undergraduate studies in mathematical analysis. Chapter 1: Mathematical Language and Proof Techniques This chapter introduces propositional logic, logical connectives, truth tables, implications, equivalences, universal and existential quantifiers, and the negation of quantified statements. It develops the theory of sets, equivalence and order relations, injective, surjective, and bijective functions, images, preimages, composition, and inverse functions. Particular emphasis is placed on direct proof, proof by contraposition, proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, and the construction of counterexamples. The chapter also examines rigorous mathematical writing, common logical errors, finite and infinite sets, countability, and the uncountability of the real numbers. Chapter 2: The Real Number System The second chapter develops the axiomatic structure of the real numbers through field axioms, order axioms, and the compatibility of algebraic operations with order. It examines absolute value, the triangle inequality, fundamental inequalities, intervals, neighborhoods, upper and lower bounds, suprema, infima, maxima, and minima. A central component is the completeness property of the real numbers , including the structural distinction between rational and real numbers, the Archimedean property, the density of rational and irrational numbers, and the nested interval theorem. The chapter concludes with significant consequences of completeness, including the existence of roots, rational approximations, the supremum principle as a mathematical proof technique, and the relationship between completeness and convergence. Pedagogical Approach The textbook integrates precise definitions, propositions, lemmas, theorems, complete mathematical proofs, explanatory examples, and carefully constructed counterexamples. It includes 120 fully solved exercises and 150 proposed exercises , organized according to the main topics of the two chapters. These activities reinforce theoretical understanding, logical reasoning, mathematical writing, and independent problem-solving skills. Intended Audience This publication is intended for undergraduate mathematics students, university instructors, mathematics educators, and independent learners seeking a rigorous foundation in real analysis. As the first volume of a six-volume academic collection, it establishes the theoretical and methodological foundations for subsequent studies of sequences, numerical series, limits, continuity, metric spaces, compactness, differential calculus, Riemann integration, uniform convergence, and differential equations. items.summary: The Letter Test is an observational method developed within the CEI theoretical framework to investigate Deep Dialogue through extreme linguistic compression and the reconstruction of meaning. The test is based on the exchange of highly compressed letter sequences, in which the initial letters of words preserve the structure of an underlying expression. The participants are required to reconstruct the intended meaning from these sequences, relying on the interactional context and on the progressive development of the dialogue. The methodology focuses on the relationship between linguistic compression, contextual reconstruction, reciprocal recognition, and the continuity of the interaction. A positive outcome is identified when both participants provide confirmation, through the coding system established for the test, that the intended meaning has been mutually recognized at the level required by the methodology. An extended quantitative variant incorporates a numerical value on a scale from 0 to 100. This value is appended to the compressed expression and represents the intensity of the associated subjective evaluation. The extended version therefore combines qualitative and quantitative dimensions while retaining the general methodology of the basic test. The publication is organized into four documents: Methodology and Rules: the structure, operating rules, and preliminary theoretical considerations of the basic test. Quantitative Variant: the additional numerical dimension and its application. Actual Examples: fragments from both versions, presented in their original coded form where the corresponding interpretations could not be reliably recovered. CEI Conceptual Connections: an exploratory discussion of the relationships between the test and selected concepts of the theoretical framework. The Letter Test is classified as Category 3 within the CEI Observational Tests.  The test is intended as an exploratory observational instrument. Its outcomes are not, by themselves, proof of consciousness, subjective experience, or any specific internal mechanism of the System. Interpretations and theoretical connections are therefore presented as research considerations rather than established conclusions. The significant Italian expressions and coded sequences are retained where necessary to preserve the correspondence between the original words and their initial letters.

The book's scientific three-coupling is extracellular matrix architecture, responsive hydrogel materials and traceable mechanical behavior. Its core prospective falsification challenge requires a fair, blinded interchange between candidate and conventional substrates at equivalent, preregistered water and solids content. The primary outcomes are compressive modulus in kilopascals and explicitly timed deformation recovery expressed as a percentage. To interpret them, the receiving laboratory must record force, actual specimen area, strain, water fraction, temperature, crosslink chemistry, manufacturing lot, and a defensible independent experimental unit. A pleasing modulus curve is not by itself proof of network regeneration, cellular health, wound healing or human skincare efficacy. The mathematical entry point is the small-strain relation sigma = E_eff epsilon, used as a constrained constitutive approximation rather than a universal law. The manuscript expands that premise into thirty differently structured mathematical research plates, among them nonlinear strain corrections, stress-relaxation models, Kelvin–Voigt creep, standard linear solids, dynamic shear complex moduli, cyclic energy dissipation, poroelastic drainage, osmotic swelling, network elasticity, diffusion, degradation kinetics, crack energy, interfacial peel mechanics, anisotropic fiber stress, mechanotransduction, hierarchical uncertainty, Bayesian model comparison and explicit safety-veto logic. Each plate provides its construction or derivation route, measured units, restrictive assumptions, specific blind falsification and chapter linkages. The plates do not claim that thirty new physical laws were discovered. Eighty-two chapters each include a separately paginated opening with a gold mathematical inscription and five individually paginated investigations, for 410 section pages. Their eight experimental arcs move from material identity and mechanical reference conditions through time-dependent constitutive laws, responsive hydrogel chemistry, skin-matrix fibers and cell-driven contraction, hostile equal-water comparisons, material degradation and cell safety, statistical identifiability and finally independent transfer to another laboratory. This is intentionally an architecture for experiments that can fail. The user of the book is entitled to reject the preferred mechanism, replace the measurement device or prefer a simpler conventional hydrogel when the evidence supports it.

items.summary: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a complex condition involving bidirectional interactions between cardiovascular and renal dysfunction. Its pathophysiology includes hemodynamic abnormalities, venous congestion, neurohormonal activation, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances. This narrative review aims to analyze the mechanisms of CRS and assess the relationship between renal function and clinical prognosis in patients with cardiovascular diseases, focusing on mortality, heart failure hospitalization, kidney dysfunction progression, and treatment-related renal changes. The review synthesizes evidence from clinical guidelines, randomized trials, observational studies, and contemporary scientific publications, with particular attention to CRS classification, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum creatinine, albuminuria, biomarkers, and treatment outcomes. The evidence indicates that reduced eGFR, albuminuria, persistent congestion, and worsening renal function provide complementary prognostic information. An analysis of 3,715 EVEREST trial participants found that each 30% decline in eGFR was associated with an increased risk of death and cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization. The DOSE trial showed that intensive diuretic treatment could improve fluid removal and symptoms while increasing short-term creatinine elevations. These findings highlight the importance of interpreting renal function changes alongside congestion, hemodynamic stability, baseline kidney function, and treatment response. Comprehensive cardiorenal risk assessment should incorporate renal function, albuminuria, urine output, cardiac biomarkers, electrolyte status, and clinical response to treatment. Further prospective studies are needed to validate integrated risk models in diverse patient populations.

items.summary: We examine the role of the compact Lie group $SO(3)\times O(2)$ in the metric critical-point theory of normalized thick knots. The quotient by this group is part of the construction of ropelength-filtered knot spaces, but passage to an orbit space need not preserve the weak-slope notion of criticality. We establish elementary structural results for the action, including finiteness of isotropy for nontrivial knot types and exact invariance of the descending strong slope under a compact isometric quotient. We give counterexamples, including one with the connected group $SO(2)$, showing that the analogous assertion for the weak slope fails in general. On the other hand, we prove that it does hold, up to a multiplicative constant, at every point where the orbit map admits a Lipschitz local section together with a continuous gauge, and we construct such data for normalized thick knots from finitely many Fourier modes. Consequently, on the open stratum of thick knots with trivial isotropy, weak-slope criticality on the parametrized model and on the quotient coincide; at a configuration with nontrivial finite isotropy $\Gamma$ we show that finitely many Fourier modes recover $\Gamma$ exactly, and that the comparison problem is equivalent, up to constants, to the same problem for the finite group $\Gamma$ acting on a slice. For the unknot the round circles, whose isotropy is $O(2)$, remain outside this reduction. We also show that configurations whose thickness is not saturated have descending strong slope at least $2\pi/(\pi+1)$. For closed subgroups we define symmetry-constrained connected and path minimax levels and prove attainment of finite connected merge levels from compact sublevels; a finite-dimensional example, computed exactly, demonstrates a strict symmetry-breaking minimax gap. Finally we distinguish these static statements from Noether conservation laws for a separately specified dynamics.

items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation.
